stories.title: Sierra Ridge Pays $31M for Phoenix Warehouse
stories.excerpt: Newmark arranged the $31 million sale of 3137 East Elwood Street, a 123,032-square-foot industrial building situated on approximately 9.8 acres in Phoenix’s Southbank Business Park, to Sierra Ridge Capital. The property was fully leased to three tenants at closing. Newmark’s Gary Cornish and Nico Burgarello, in collaboration with Barry Gabel, CJ Osbrink and Chris Marchildon, led the assignment on behalf of Sierra Ridge Capital. The transaction marks the culmination of a full-cycle assignment for the Newmark team, which originally sold the property to the current seller in 2024. During the approximately two-year hold period, ownership completed a significant office-to-industrial conversion and capital improvement program, transforming the asset into a highly functional industrial facility. Newmark subsequently leased the building to full occupancy before facilitating its sale on behalf of the same client.  “This sale is a great example of what a well-executed office-to-industrial conversion can deliver,” said Cornish. “We had the privilege of selling this building to our client in 2024, and in roughly two years they transformed it into a fully leased, highly functional industrial asset. Sierra Ridge Capital recognized how rare it is to find 100% HVAC space with heavy power, secured yard space and heavy industrial zoning in a central infill location with immediate freeway access.”  “3137 East Elwood is exactly what we are focused on acquiring at Sierra Ridge Capital: a highly functional industrial building in a central infill location where developable land is scarce,” said Nick Angelich, Co-Managing Partner at Sierra Ridge Capital. “Its power, gated yard and full HVAC meet the needs of traditional distribution, contractor and service users, as well as the advanced manufacturing and technology companies reshaping Phoenix’s economy. We appreciate Gary and the Newmark team for delivering a clean, off-market execution, and we are excited to continue growi
bullets: Sierra Ridge Capital purchased fully-leased 123,032-sf industrial building Phoenix for $31M
Prior owner completed office-to-industrial conversion during 2-year hold; asset now fully leased
Newmark facilitated sale after delivering full occupancy; marks arbitrage on asset class conversion
stories.summary: Sierra Ridge Capital acquired a 123,032-square-foot industrial property in Phoenix's Southbank Business Park for $31 million at full occupancy. The previous owner executed a office-to-industrial conversion and capital improvement program during a roughly two-year hold, transforming the asset into a fully leased, highly functional industrial facility. The transaction demonstrates strong demand for converted industrial stock in Phoenix and successful value creation through adaptive reuse.
stories.impact: Office-to-industrial conversions are capturing market inefficiency in Phoenix as e-commerce and logistics demand absorb vacant or underperforming office stock. This signals sustained industrial strength in Phoenix but also tight industrial fundamentals pushing investors to compete for conversions rather than new ground-up development—a constraint on greenfield multifamily land availability in submarkets with overlapping industrial/mixed-use development opportunity.

stories.title: Hillpointe Building 358-Unit Reno Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Hillpointe acquired a 32.5-acre site at 18610 Wedge Parkway in South Reno, on which it will build a 358-home rental community called Pointe Grand Cape at Southport. Pointe Grand Cape at Southport will feature 268 two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartments across 12 residential buildings, along with 90 built-to-rent three-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bathroom townhomes, each with an attached two-car garage. The community will feature a clubhouse, along with a resort-style pool and hot tub, a fully equipped fitness center, a dedicated dog park and a pickleball court. The community’s location is just 5 to 10 minutes from The Summit Reno, one of the area’s premier shopping, dining and lifestyle destinations. Grading at Pointe Grand Cape at Southport will begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with full site work starting in December and vertical construction anticipated in March 2027. Following first deliveries in January 2028, the community is slated for completion in April 2028. Hillpointe was represented by Ryan Kruger of Land Advisors Organization in the transaction.  The post Hillpointe Building 358-Unit Reno Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hillpointe acquired 32.5-acre South Reno site; 358-unit rental community (268 apartments + 90 townhomes)
Grading Q4 2026, vertical construction March 2027, first deliveries January 2028, completion April 2028
Prime location 5–10 minutes from The Summit Reno; resort-style amenities and built-to-rent townhomes
stories.summary: Hillpointe acquired a 32.5-acre parcel in South Reno for a 358-home rental community called Pointe Grand Cape at Southport, comprising 268 two-bedroom apartments and 90 three-bedroom townhomes with garages. Construction timeline starts grading Q4 2026, with vertical construction in March 2027 and deliveries beginning January 2028. The community is positioned near The Summit Reno, a major retail and lifestyle destination, and features resort-style amenities and dedicated townhome inventory.
stories.impact: Reno's rental market remains supply-constrained and demand-strong, with built-to-rent townhomes commanding significant pipeline allocation. Hillpointe's move signals confidence in Reno's continued in-migration (remote work, California displacement) and willingness to develop spec inventory at scale. The 18-month construction timeline reflects favorable cost and labor conditions; similar market tightness will accelerate local wage inflation and material pricing into 2027–2028.

stories.title: Entertainment Firm Fifth Season Grabs 5K SF at 115 West 27th Street
stories.excerpt: Lights, camera, (office) action! Fifth Season, a global media company that develops, finances, produces and distributes movies, television shows and documentaries, has signed a 5,000-square-foot lease at 115 West 27th Street in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, sources confirmed to Commercial Observer. The deal, first reported by Traded, was signed Oct. 12. The length of the lease was not immediately available, but the asking rent was $45 per square foot, according to the source. Michael Gammal and Avery Reavill from KSR brokered the deal for the tenant, as well as for landlord Joel Berman. Gammal and Reavil declined to comment, while Fifth Season did not immediately respond to CO’s request for comment. The deal seems to represent a relocation from 60 Madison Avenue for Fifth Season, which rebranded from its former name Endeavor Content in 2022. The entertainment company has other offices in L.A. and London and distributes some of the world’s most popular television shows and movies, including “East of Eden,” “Severance,” “Killing Eve,” “Nonnas” and “In the Heights.” Built in 1910, 115 West 27th Street is a 12-story boutique loft-style office building about three blocks northwest of Madison Square Park. Other tenants at 115 West 27th Street include fitness studio Body & Pole, mental health technology and telehealth provider BH OpCo Inc., as well as brand management firm Stag & Hare. Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Fifth Season (media/entertainment) signed 5,000-sf lease Chelsea Manhattan at $45/sf asking rent
Lease executed Oct. 12; represents relocation from 60 Madison Avenue; tenure term undisclosed
Company operates offices in LA and London; no employment headcount data provided
stories.summary: Fifth Season, a global media company producing and distributing films and television, leased 5,000 square feet at 115 West 27th Street in Manhattan's Chelsea for $45 per square foot. The deal, brokered by KSR's Michael Gammal and Avery Reavill, appears to represent a relocation from the company's prior 60 Madison Avenue location. No lease term or specific headcount was disclosed.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily demand. This is a single-tenant office relocation within Manhattan, not a net job influx or corporate expansion. The $45/sf rent in Chelsea reflects soft office conditions; no signal of employer growth driving residential demand in any specific metro.

stories.title: ESJ Inks Acquisition Loan for 144-Unit Kannapolis Rental Asset
stories.excerpt: ESJ Partners utilized a $19.9 million loan to finance the acquisition of The Bridges of Cabarrus, a 2021-vintage garden-style multifamily community comprising 144 units across seven three-story buildings in Kannapolis, North Carolina. The property sold for $29.5 million. Pickering & Co. was the seller. The loan was originated and structured on behalf of Pearlmark Realty Senior Mortgage Partners, led by Brian Johnson. The company provided a fixed-rate, senior mortgage. A JLL team led by Brian Gaswirth arranged the financing. The Bridges at Cabarrus features amenities such as a clubhouse, fitness center, pool, and 294 parking spaces. The property is in Cabarrus County, approximately 25 miles from Uptown Charlotte. ESJ Capital Partners is a vertically integrated real estate investment firm with a focus on middle-market investments, with over 50 realized transactions representing more than $280 million in total equity.  The post ESJ Inks Acquisition Loan for 144-Unit Kannapolis Rental Asset appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: ESJ Partners acquired 144-unit garden-style community Kannapolis, NC for $29.5M; financed with $19.9M loan
Pearlmark Realty Senior Mortgage Partners provided fixed-rate senior mortgage; JLL arranged
Property delivered 2021; situated 25 miles from Uptown Charlotte in Cabarrus County
stories.summary: ESJ Partners financed the acquisition of The Bridges of Cabarrus, a 144-unit garden-style multifamily community in Kannapolis, North Carolina, using a $19.9 million senior mortgage from Pearlmark Realty. The property sold for $29.5 million and was delivered in 2021. The asset is located approximately 25 miles from Uptown Charlotte and features standard garden-style amenities.
stories.impact: Financing activity for secondary-market garden-style inventory in the Charlotte orbit (Kannapolis is mid-market, not core) suggests lenders remain active on stabilized, performing assets outside the primary metros. Low leverage (67%) and fixed-rate terms indicate disciplined underwriting; no signal of market stress or demand deterioration in the Charlotte region, though acquisition pricing and terms do not suggest aggressive development or rent growth ahead.

stories.title: Meritex Recapitalizes 18-Building Atlanta Warehouse Portfolio
stories.excerpt: The Meritex Company recapitalized select assets in partnership with funds managed by Vintage Strategies at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. The newly formed continuation vehicle acquired exposure to an 18-building infill industrial portfolio totaling 1,222,596 square feet in Atlanta, GA. Under the terms of the transaction, Meritex will remain as the controlling partner and will serve as the operating member and day-to-day manager of the portfolio. The portfolio consists of multi-tenant shallow- and mid-bay industrial properties in the Northeast, North Central/Georgia-400 and Northwest submarkets of Atlanta. The properties are situated in Kennesaw, Smyrna, Norcross, Lawrenceville, and Alpharetta. Serving a diverse tenant base across a broad range of industries, the properties benefit from strong market fundamentals, including limited availability of developable land and sustained demand for distribution and light manufacturing space. As a result, the portfolio is expected to benefit from long-term occupancy stability and continued operating performance. The post Meritex Recapitalizes 18-Building Atlanta Warehouse Portfolio appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Meritex recapitalized 18-building Atlanta industrial portfolio (1.23M sf) with Goldman Sachs Alternatives funds
Multi-tenant shallow/mid-bay infill industrial; spread across Northeast, North Central, Northwest Atlanta/suburbs
Portfolio includes Kennesaw, Smyrna, Norcross, Lawrenceville, Alpharetta; limited developable land, sustained demand
stories.summary: Meritex Company formed a continuation vehicle with Goldman Sachs Alternatives to recapitalize an 18-building industrial portfolio totaling 1.23 million square feet across Atlanta's submarkets (Kennesaw, Smyrna, Norcross, Lawrenceville, Alpharetta). Meritex remains the controlling partner and operating member. The portfolio is multi-tenant shallow/mid-bay space serving distribution and light manufacturing tenants.
stories.impact: Continued investor appetite for Atlanta infill industrial reflects sustained logistics demand and limited land availability in the region. However, recapitalization (not new acquisition or development) signals mature, cash-flowing assets attracting alt-asset capital rather than speculative development. Scarcity of Atlanta industrial land noted in the deal thesis is relevant: land constraints that limit industrial supply growth also constrain multifamily ground-up opportunities in the same in-fill submarkets, particularly around I-285 and I-75 corridors.

stories.title: Embrey Scores $76.2M Financing for 354-Unit Orlando Apartment Community
stories.excerpt: Embrey obtained $76.2 million in construction take-out financing for Citron at The Packing District, a 354-unit, Class A multifamily community in Orlando, Florida. Newmark engaged the bridge-lending market, debt funds, balance-sheet lenders, and CLO-driven capital sources to secure the financing. Newmark’s Matthew Williams and Rob Wright secured the financing on behalf of EMBREY, with support from Kyle Schlitt, James Maynard and David Williams. Delivered in 2025, Citron at The Packing District comprises a five-story residential building and adjoining six-story structured parking garage. Residential amenities include a media room, a pool with an adjacent aqua lounge and poolside cabanas, and a WiFi lounge with a conference room and dedicated micro-offices. Located within The Packing District, a $700 million, 202-acre mixed-use redevelopment, Citron offers convenient access to retail, dining and employment centers, including Publix Super Market, the Great Southern Box Company food hall and the nearby College Park and Edgewater Drive neighborhoods. The post Embrey Scores $76.2M Financing for 354-Unit Orlando Apartment Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Embrey secured $76.2M construction take-out financing for 354-unit Class A Orlando apartment community
Citron at The Packing District delivered 2025; 5-story residential + 6-story parking garage structure
Located within $700M, 202-acre mixed-use redevelopment; access to retail, dining, employment centers
stories.summary: Embrey obtained $76.2 million in construction take-out financing for Citron at The Packing District, a 354-unit Class A apartment community in Orlando that delivered in 2025. The project comprises a five-story residential building and six-story structured parking garage. Newmark engaged bridge lenders, debt funds, balance-sheet lenders, and CLO capital to secure the financing. The property is situated within The Packing District, a $700 million mixed-use redevelopment on 202 acres.
stories.impact: Successful take-out financing for a 2025-delivered Class A Orlando asset signals continued appetite for market-rate multifamily in growth metros, even as construction lending tightened in 2023–2024. The mix of capital sources (CLO-driven, balance-sheet, debt funds) indicates healthy secondary market for stabilized product. Orlando's continued in-migration and employment growth support rent resilience, but market has added significant supply; this deal's success depends on continued migration velocity to the metro and Orlando's submarket differentials.

stories.title: Your Family Lives There. So Why Is New York Imposing a Pied-à-Terre Tax?
stories.excerpt: Across New York City, high-value real estate is commonly held through trusts and limited liability companies (LLCs), which serve important purposes, from estate planning to privacy and liability protection. Yet, many families are discovering that the ownership arrangements their advisers recommended for these purposes now trigger the city’s pied-à-terre tax — even when the “owner” or a family member is the primary, full-time resident. Consider a common scenario. Parents establish a trust to hold a Manhattan apartment for their three children. One child makes the apartment her primary residence. The other two live elsewhere. On its face, the property appears exempt from the pied-à-terre tax. After all, someone lives there full time as a primary resident. Adam Margulies. Photo: Courtesy Farrell Fritz. In actuality, when a trust has multiple beneficiaries, the beneficial interest in trust property is shared among them. The resident child is not the sole beneficial owner — she holds an undivided interest alongside her nonresident siblings. And the trust itself, not being a natural person, cannot have a “residence.” The result is the tax would apply. The practical impact extends beyond the tax itself. Friction may develop among beneficiaries over who should bear a tax triggered by one beneficiary’s occupancy, leaving the trustees in a difficult position over whether to use trust funds to pay a tax that benefits only one beneficiary. A second common arrangement is the “stacked” structure, in which an LLC holds title and is wholly owned by a trust. This layering offers the liability shield and anonymity of the LLC (whose sole asset is the property) along with the estate tax benefits of the trust. From a pied-à-terre tax perspective, however, the extra layer is a problem. The legal owner is the LLC, which, like a trust, is not a natural person and cannot have a residence of its own. bullets: NYC pied-à-terre tax applies to trust/LLC-held residential property even with primary resident occupant
Tax triggered when beneficial interest fractured among multiple beneficiaries; trust itself has no 'residence'
Estate planning structures recommended pre-tax now unintentionally trigger pied-à-terre tax liability
stories.summary: New York City's pied-à-terre tax increasingly applies to residential properties held in trusts or LLCs even when a beneficiary is the primary resident, because beneficial interest is shared and trusts cannot hold a 'residence.' A common scenario—parents establishing a trust for three children with one child as primary resident—triggers tax liability on the entire property. This unintended consequence of estate planning and privacy structures has created confusion and tax exposure for high-net-worth Manhattan property owners.
stories.impact: Pied-à-terre tax enforcement and interpretation shifts create uncertainty and friction in NYC's high-value residential market, deterring capital inflow and creating disincentives for multi-generational wealth holds in Manhattan. Reduced investor appetite for Manhattan condo/rental purchases as principal residences (fear of tax recharacterization on secondary beneficiaries) may compress prime Manhattan rental rates and reduce capital for high-end multifamily development. Secondary impact: developers may face pressure to offer smaller, lower-cost units if affluent owner-occupants retreat.

stories.title: Power Availability Defining Most Coveted Locations in CRE
stories.excerpt: A surge in demand for artificial intelligence has transformed the importance of location in commercial real estate transactions. Markets with sufficient energy access and broadband connections coupled with the ability to quickly produce new power sources could gain advantages in attracting CRE investment, according to a new report from the Urban Land Institute (ULI) and Heitman shared exclusively with Commercial Observer. The ULI-Heitman report noted that global data center investment is projected to reach $7.6 trillion by 2030, with $3 trillion directly connected to real estate. Other property sectors that could benefit from the new real estate economics, according to the report, include pre-approved powered land, battery storage properties and industrial facilities. “Many times over it’s been thought that real estate value was driven by location, location, location, but increasingly access to reliable, deliverable power is becoming another critical determinant of where development can occur and where capital’s flowing,” Laura Craft, global head of portfolio sustainability strategies at Heitman, told CO. “In many markets today the demand exists, but does the power also exist to support the growth?” Aimee Witteman, chief impact officer at ULI, said Pittsburgh and part of the industrial Midwest will be well positioned to benefit from the new AI-driven real estate environment given their legacy infrastructure assets including transmission connections, substations and former manufacturing sites. Witteman stressed, though, that the amount of power won’t be all that wins the day. Markets that make the smartest use of their existing electrical grid will also benefit due to real estate development. bullets: Global data center investment projected $7.6T by 2030; $3T directly tied to real estate
AI-driven demand reshapes CRE location economics; reliable power access now primary driver vs. traditional location
Industrial, battery storage, and powered land increasingly coveted; markets with energy infrastructure gain investment advantage
stories.summary: A new ULI-Heitman report reveals that AI-driven data center demand is fundamentally reshaping commercial real estate location economics. Global data center investment is projected to reach $7.6 trillion by 2030, with $3 trillion directly connected to real estate. Access to reliable, deliverable power has become the primary location variable, displacing traditional location-location-location thinking. Markets with strong energy infrastructure, broadband, and capacity for rapid power generation (Texas, parts of Virginia) are attracting outsized capital flows.
stories.impact: Power availability is now a primary site-selection criterion for large industrial, battery, and data center projects, which competes for land with multifamily development in key markets (Texas, Midwest, Southeast). Developers in power-constrained markets (CA, parts of Northeast) face higher infrastructure costs and longer entitlement timelines. Markets with excess generation capacity (Texas) will attract large-footprint industrial and tech tenants, driving job growth and multifamily in-migration; however, speculative power-hungry data center zoning may cannibalize residentially zoned land or raise land costs in competing uses. Reno, Austin, Dallas, Phoenix submarkets near transmission infrastructure will see accelerated industrial/powered land premiums.

stories.title: Get to Know the Broker: Patrick Southern of Serhant
stories.excerpt: If you need a place in New Jersey, SERHANT’s Patrick Southern is the agent you call. In 2025 alone, he closed 376 contracts in the state, mostly in Jersey City, just a stone’s throw from the bustling luxury residential market that is Manhattan. He’s a Jersey guy at heart, and wants to take the post-pandemic boom Jersey City has seen and extend it so the area becomes just as coveted as its neighbor across the Hudson River. That’s a project he’s doing at Serhant, with the help of CEO and founder Ryan Serhant. Commercial Observer spoke with Southern in September for a series called “Get to Know the Broker,” where we learn more about residential brokers and what makes them tick. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: What has been the biggest deal of your career so far? Patrick Southern: When I was hired to sell the Dixon Advisory portfolio. I was chosen to help a giant hedge fund unwind their portfolio. I had to navigate the sale of about 700 properties. It was not your average job, to say the least. I was responsible for figuring out how to sell all 700, in what order, at what price, and how to do it efficiently. The goal was obvious: sell for the most money, quickly, without cannibalizing ourselves with our own inventory. It was a great challenge, and we successfully sold out the portfolio, with our last few units now on the market. On top of that, marrying the private sales side of the business (me) with a large corporate setup was its own challenge. But I stuck to my approach and eventually got them to understand the importance of speed and timing. We became a great team once the right leadership was in place. That project still ranks among the most interesting things I’ve done in this business. What is your career Everest? I’m building a new development business with Ryan Serhant here in New Jersey, and my goal for unit count under commitment is a big one. I’m streamlined, disciplined and plan-oriente
bullets: Patrick Southern (SERHANT) closed 376 residential contracts in New Jersey in 2025 alone
Focus on Jersey City luxury market; positioned as 'Hudson River alternative' to Manhattan
Broker leveraging post-pandemic Jersey City momentum to expand regional market perception
stories.summary: SERHANT broker Patrick Southern closed 376 residential contracts in New Jersey in 2025, primarily in Jersey City. Southern, working with CEO Ryan Serhant, aims to position Jersey City as an increasingly coveted luxury residential market rivaling Manhattan. The article profiles Southern's career, noting his prior success liquidating a 700-property hedge fund portfolio.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development strategy. This is a residential brokerage profile, not a market-structure or supply signal. Jersey City's post-pandemic desirability is well-established; no new data on rents, absorption, supply pipeline, or job growth provided. The volume figure (376 contracts) is retail residential, not multifamily.

stories.title: Scarcity, Privacy and Authenticity Are Luxury Development’s Calling Cards Now
stories.excerpt: The standard of luxury in residential real estate has traditionally been measured by what can be seen and counted: square footage, ceiling heights, the number of amenities, or the length of the services list. But today’s discerning buyers are increasingly drawn to the experiential qualities of a home: how it feels to move through the space, the sense of privacy and calm it provides, its connection to its surroundings, and how thoughtfully it supports daily life. In New York City, where space is inherently scarce, and neighborhoods have distinct histories and identities, the most valuable qualities of a home are often the ones that cannot be easily replicated. Privacy, authenticity, craftsmanship and a genuine sense of place are becoming the new markers of luxury. Shlomi Avdoo. PHOTO: Courtesy Avdoo That shift is one we have seen firsthand at Avdoo. From the beginning, we have believed that every project should respond to its neighborhood rather than follow a generic formula. We begin by studying the history, architecture and character of the site, then assemble a team of architects, interior designers and landscape designers whose perspectives are suited to that specific place. At our Bergen condominium project, we collaborated with Taller Frida Escobedo, DXA Studio and Workstead to create a building rooted in the character of Boerum Hill and the creative culture of Brooklyn. The architecture, interiors, landscape, and programming were conceived together to establish a distinct residential experience that reflects its surroundings. At 110 Boerum Place, we worked with local architect Brent Buck and Brook Landscape to balance the privacy and expansiveness of a Cobble Hill townhouse with the conveniences of a full-service condominium. Working with a team deeply familiar with the neighborhood allowed us to approach the building with sensitivity to the scale and character of the surrounding streetscape. bullets: Luxury residential buyers shift from quantitative (sf, amenities, services) to experiential (privacy, craftsmanship, authenticity)
NYC-specific trend: scarcity, neighborhood history, place-making now premium differentiators over unit counts
Developer strategy pivots to site-specific design and authentic placemaking vs. formulaic luxury programming
stories.summary: Luxury residential developers in New York City report a fundamental shift in buyer preferences away from quantitative measures (square footage, amenities, service counts) toward experiential qualities: privacy, craftsmanship, authentic neighborhood connection, and sense of place. Scarcity and neighborhood-responsive design are emerging as primary luxury markers. Developers like Avdoo are prioritizing site-specific architecture and placemaking over generic, replicated luxury amenity packages.
stories.impact: This signals demand-side segmentation within NYC high-end residential market—buyers willing to pay premium for authenticity and scarcity over standardized luxury. For multifamily developers, this suggests upside pricing power in neighborhood-sensitive, smaller-scale projects (boutique, limited units, bespoke design) vs. large-format, amenity-heavy product. However, it also reflects buyer sophistication and willingness to trade density/service for privacy and place, which may constrain density and unit yields on boutique deals. Broader implication: luxury rental and sale markets are polarizing; generic mid-luxury towers face competitive pressure, while truly differentiated, limited-supply projects command premiums.
